source: Wikipedia (2026 text) Conceptual blending; summarising Fauconnier and Turner (1998)
finding: The blending network has four kinds of space. Input spaces hold the specific content. A generic space holds structure common to both inputs. A cross-space mapping links counterparts. The blended space gets selected parts of both inputs by selective projection.
numbers: Network has at least 4 spaces. Emergent structure comes from 3 operations: composition, completion, elaboration. Theory development began 1993; Koestler's 1964 bisociation is the named forerunner.
limits: Secondary source (Wikipedia), not the 1998 Cognitive Science paper itself. The page says the theory does not explain where the inputs to a blend come from.
agent_relevance: These are the data fields a coded blend operator needs: two inputs, a generic space, a mapping, a projection filter, and a blend object. The missing input-selection step must come from the program, not the theory.

source: Wikipedia (2026 text) Conceptual blending; Buddhist monk riddle after Koestler (1964)
finding: Worked example: a monk climbs a mountain one day and descends another. Blend the two days into one day with two monks on the same path. Running the blend shows they must meet, which proves a shared place and hour exists.
numbers: Two inputs (ascent day, descent day). Day and path are merged; the two monks stay separate. One counterpart pair (monk to monk). No experiment, a worked riddle.
limits: A hand-picked riddle, not a test. No data on how often people find the blend or whether blends beat other methods.
agent_relevance: Template for the 'run the blend' step (elaboration): simulate the merged scene and read off the consequence. Code can check the consequence against the original problem statement.

source: Wikipedia (2026 text) Conceptual blending; network types
finding: Four network types: simplex (one input is a frame, the other holds values), mirror (a shared frame), single-scope (different frames, one is projected), double-scope (both frames contribute).
numbers: 4 types listed. The monk riddle is given as a mirror example.
limits: Typology is descriptive. No study in the page measures which type gives better solutions.
agent_relevance: A blend operator can offer a type switch: first try single-scope (cheaper, one frame leads), try double-scope only after a check fails. This is a design choice [D], not an evidence-backed rule.

source: Wikipedia (2026 text) Conceptual blending; computational models paragraph
finding: Lists the computational lineage: Shrager's 1980s 'view application' (the early name for blending), Guhe et al. 2011 for basic mathematics, later structure-mapping based models, and Lieto and Pozzato's typicality logic for pet-fish style combinations and blending.
numbers: Citations given: Shrager 1987 Machine Learning 2(3):247-276; Guhe et al. 2011 Cogn Syst Res 12(3-4):249-265; Lieto and Pozzato 2020 JETAI 32(5):769-804.
limits: Wikipedia says Shrager's model predates the theory. Page offers no performance numbers for any program.
agent_relevance: Confirms the three families to read: frame merging (Shrager), analogy plus generalisation (Guhe, HDTP), and logic-based typicality (Lieto).

source: Shrager (1987) Theory Change via View Application in Instructionless Learning, Machine Learning 2:247-276
finding: Empirical base of the earliest blend program: 7 CMU undergraduates tried to figure out a programmable toy tank (BigTrak) with no instructions. All built a mostly correct theory in 30 to 45 minutes.
numbers: N=7. 33 to 68 interactions per person (mean 52, SD 12.9). Mean gap between interactions 27.7 s (SD 5.7). Theory sessions 30 to 45 min.
limits: Very small N, one device, one lab. The human data come from Shrager and Klahr (1986), only summarised here. No statistics beyond descriptives.
agent_relevance: Shows the human pattern the operator copies: theory changes happen on surprise, from what the device actually did, not from analysis of why the prediction failed. This matches our rule G2 (revise from real output).

source: Shrager (1987) view application: six empirical generalisations from the BigTrak protocols
finding: Theory changes came when the device did something unexpected or a new part was considered; learners used the positive behaviour seen, not blame analysis; changes were sometimes non-monotonic; sizes were uneven; they drew on outside knowledge such as a clock face; and changes were coherent (one change touched many aspects).
numbers: Example: learning the toy is 'programmable' changed several operations and model knowledge together. Turn units were minutes of a clock (15 units = 90 degrees).
limits: Generalisations are qualitative, from 7 protocols. Authors admit no principled theory of which outside knowledge (view) gets picked.
agent_relevance: Supports one big structured jump per reframe instead of many small edits. Also warns: view selection is the unsolved part, so the agent needs an explicit, logged selection rule.

source: Shrager (1987) view application: the five-step algorithm
finding: To apply a view: (1) copy the view as a base; (2) merge the current theory into it by matching frames of the same type (ambiguous matches resolved at random); (3) coerce child frames to their new parent type; (4) fill uninstantiated view slots from the theory; (5) enforce that each object plays a role in only one operation.
numbers: 5 steps. Ambiguous match picks 'at random'. Single-function assumption is step 5.
limits: Heuristics for coercion are hand-written and domain specific. Random tie-breaking is a stated weakness.
agent_relevance: Closest published recipe for a coded blend: copy, match, coerce, fill, de-duplicate. A program can run all 5 steps and the LLM only fills slots (match proposal, coercion wording). Matches, conflicts and a final consistency check stay in code.

source: Shrager (1987) view application: the eight views used in IE
finding: IE had only eight hand-made views, each taken from what subjects used: CODE.AND.STARTUP, CLEAR, SIMPLE.CODED.DEVICE, SIMPLE.PROGRAMMING, COMMAND.ARGUMENT, MODE.SHIFT, BASIC, VECTOR.COMPRESSION.
numbers: 8 views; the search analysis assumes 6 views with 2 object frames and 2 operation frames each.
limits: Views were added when the authors saw a subject use one, so the model is fitted to its own protocols (circular).
agent_relevance: A small curated library of reusable abstractions beats an open search. For our agent, a library of 'views' (known solution patterns) would be mined from solved tasks, not invented by the model on the fly.

source: Shrager (1987) search analysis of view application versus single-frame edits
finding: View application makes each step bigger but keeps only coherent theories. Counting: 960 successors per theory at the second view, 5,760 theories after two views. The single-frame space needs about eight steps to match the same two view steps and holds about 124 million theories.
numbers: 5,760 vs about 124,000,000 alternatives (second view level vs eighth simple level). Estimate 60k^4 theories after k view applications. 96 theories at level 2 of the simple space.
limits: Back-of-envelope counts from assumed sizes (6 views, 2+2 frames, branching factor 10). Not measured on data. Author notes the actual search is hill climbing (credit to Langley).
agent_relevance: Argument for coherence-preserving jumps: a blend operator prunes incoherent candidates before they reach the model. Gives a cost model for how many candidate blends to expect per step.

source: Shrager (1987) view application: fit to human sessions
finding: In cognitive-model mode IE could track a subject for up to 6 view applications (12 interactions) without help from causal reasoning, and about 3 times that (about 30 interactions) when the causal analysis was supplied by hand.
numbers: Human sessions: about 52 interactions. IE: 12 interactions auto, about 30 with manual causal analysis.
limits: Model was matched to individual protocols with hand-chosen view and match decisions. It does not predict new subjects. Causal analyser handled only specific cases.
agent_relevance: Honest limit: even the best early blend program needed a human to supply the failure analysis. In our agent the failure analysis is the code-run check (G2), which fits.

source: Shrager (1987) view application: generality tests and assumptions
finding: The representation was also used for a CD player, a microwave oven and a digital watch. It assumes deterministic devices, one function per operation, low cost of interaction and rich behaviour to cue views. It would fail on a costly, low-feedback system such as air traffic control.
numbers: 4 devices in total (BigTrak plus 3 simplified simulations).
limits: Simulations removed much of real device richness (sounds and movements became symbols like BEEP). No external evaluation.
agent_relevance: Boundary: blend-and-test works when trying a candidate is cheap and the output is informative. Our tasks with code execution meet this; tasks with no cheap check do not.

source: Shrager (1987) view application: wrong but coherent theories
finding: Coherent does not mean correct. Applying the BASIC (addressable memory) view to a digital watch makes IE expect a program memory the watch lacks. The wrong theory stays until a later view reassigns the parts.
numbers: One worked example (digital watch plus BASIC view).
limits: Single anecdote, no rate of such errors measured.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G3: a coherent blend still needs a test on something the blend was not fitted to. Plausible structure is not proof.

source: Lieto and Pozzato (2020) A description logic framework for commonsense conceptual combination (TCL), JETAI
finding: TCL is a nonmonotonic description logic (ALC+TR with probabilistic typicality inclusions p::T(C) subset D). It combines two prototypes by building scenarios, throwing out inconsistent ones, and preferring features of the HEAD concept over the MODIFIER. It handles the 'pet fish' problem (prototype of pet fish is not a mix of pet and fish prototypes).
numbers: Reasoning is EXPTIME-complete, same as plain ALC. Worked scenario tables: e.g. Stone+Lion has top scenarios at 28.22% and 12.10%; the selected scenario has 3.02% and yields HardMaterial 0.9, MainColorGreyish 0.8, has.Tail 0.7.
limits: No human data in this paper. Probabilities and typicality weights are hand-set in the knowledge base. HEAD/MODIFIER must be assigned by hand (footnote: no general automatic method).
agent_relevance: A clean, checkable combination rule: take all consistent head features, add modifier features that do not conflict, choose by probability. This can be coded as the 'project selectively' step with the LLM only proposing candidate features.

source: Lieto and Pozzato (2020) TCL: creative uses (anti-hero, chimera, stone lion) and iteration
finding: TCL generates new character concepts by combining TvTropes descriptions: ANTI-HERO from HERO and VILLAIN, an anti-hero chimera, a stone lion. Outputs can be fed back into TCL to combine already combined concepts.
numbers: Anti-hero chimera result keeps 0.9 probability for has.Tail, has.Horns, has.Beards, FireBreathing, Aggressive and 0.95 for Protagonist. Top trivial scenario holds 20.4% and is discarded.
limits: Illustration only. No test that the generated concepts are novel, useful or liked by people. Authors state it is hard to say what the 'correct' combination is in creativity.
agent_relevance: Shows the pipeline 'enumerate, drop trivial and inconsistent, pick by score' on knowledge-base inputs. The 'drop the trivial scenario' rule (inherit-everything-from-the-head is not a blend) is a cheap code check for non-blends.

source: Lieto and Pozzato (2020) TCL: related-work comparison with blending systems
finding: Authors place TCL next to two logic-based blending systems: Confalonieri et al. (2016) uses description logic EL++ and an upward refinement operator to build the generic space; Eppe et al. (2018) casts generalisation as a nonmonotonic search solved with answer set programming. They say TCL covers blending but note there is no evidence that the other two handle pet-fish type problems.
numbers: Cites Confalonieri et al. 2016 (EL++), Eppe et al. 2018 (ASP), Nagai and Taura 2006 (combination vs blending).
limits: Authors compare their own system; claims about the others are about coverage, not measured performance. Blending vs combination difference: blending yields an entirely novel concept with weak ties to the inputs.
agent_relevance: Maps the design space: generic-space search (EL++, ASP), property-inheritance logic (TCL), frame merging (Shrager). All three keep the program in charge and use logic as the checker.

source: Eppe, Maclean, Confalonieri, Kutz, Schorlemmer, Plaza, Kuhnberger (2018) A computational framework for conceptual blending, Artificial Intelligence 256
finding: Framework treats generalisation of the input concepts as a search problem solved with answer set programming, and prunes the space of blends with metrics that capture most of the optimality principles of blending theory. Demonstrated on invented concepts in mathematics and music.
numbers: Semantic Scholar lists 87 citations (retrieved 2026-11-01). Full paper not opened: the publisher PDF returned 403.
limits: Abstract only. Domains are mathematics and music proofs of concept; no human evaluation of the blends is stated in the abstract.
agent_relevance: Best formal template for a coded blend operator: generalise by search, score by explicit optimality metrics, prune. Read the full paper for the metric definitions before copying.

source: Cardoso and Pereira et al. (2019) The nuts and bolts of conceptual blending: multidomain concept creation with Divago, in Computational Synthesis and Creative Systems
finding: Divago is described as one of the first computational blending systems. The chapter covers its architecture from the late 1990s sketch to a mature 2005 version and its concept-creation experiments.
numbers: No numbers read. Related paper: Pereira and Cardoso (2006) Experiments with free concept generation in Divago, Knowledge-Based Systems (DOI 10.1016/j.knosys.2006.04.008).
limits: Abstract page only; full text not opened (paywall). Author list of the chapter not verified. Details such as the genetic-algorithm search over blends remain unverified.
agent_relevance: Divago remains the main named design to copy; read the full chapter before building. Do not cite its internals from this line.

source: Veale (2019) From conceptual mash-ups to badass blends: a robust computational model of conceptual blending, in Computational Synthesis and Creative Systems
finding: Introduces the 'conceptual mash-up': a robust, shallow form of blending that reuses a program's commonsense knowledge, with that knowledge harvested automatically from the web by mining the casual questions people ask.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Abstract page only. Author attribution (Veale) from background knowledge, not verified in this session.
agent_relevance: A pragmatic precedent: use cheap, robust property-level blending over a mined knowledge store instead of full structure mapping. Fits an LLM that supplies the properties.

source: Amalgams, colimits and conceptual blending, in Computational Synthesis and Creative Systems (2018)
finding: Reviews Goguen's category-theoretic blending and proposes modelling a blend as an amalgam (originally a case-based-reasoning method for knowledge transfer), then generalises the amalgam model to a colimit so it can be computed.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Abstract page only; authors not verified.
agent_relevance: Amalgam = keep the largest consistent part of each input and combine. This is a simple definable target for a 'selective projection' routine with a consistency checker.

source: The relationship between conceptual blending and analogical reasoning, in Computational Synthesis and Creative Systems (2018)
finding: Combines generalisation-based analogy (HDTP) with amalgams from case-based reasoning into a computational-level blend model, and shows an algorithmic instance that rebuilds the horse-plus-bird blend that gives Pegasus.
numbers: One worked example (Pegasus). No numbers read. A 2017 Connection Science paper (DOI 10.1080/09540091.2017.1326463) gives a related account.
limits: Abstract page only; authors not verified.
agent_relevance: Ties blending to analogy: the cross-space mapping is an analogy. Our existing schema note (O7) already says unaided analogy rarely transfers, so any mapping needs a code check.

source: Guhe, Pease, Smaill, Martinez, Schmidt, Gust, Kuhnberger, Krumnack (2011) A computational account of conceptual blending in basic mathematics, Cognitive Systems Research 12(3-4):249-265
finding: Named in Wikipedia as the main mathematics blending model. Only citation metadata was read this session, no findings.
numbers: 47 citations on Semantic Scholar (retrieved 2026-11-01). No findings read.
limits: Metadata only. The publisher page blocks automatic download; any claim about its content (HDTP-based, arithmetic domains) is background knowledge and must be verified.
agent_relevance: Gap to close: read the paper for how the generic space and blend were computed and what they tested.

source: Diaconescu (2017) 3/2-institutions: an institution theory for conceptual blending, arXiv 1708.09675
finding: Gives a category-theoretic basis for blending. Goguen modelled concepts as logical theories (axiomatised in OBJ), and blending as a lax cocone in a '3/2-category' where arrows are partial theory morphisms; whether the cocone should be a colimit (minimal) is still open. The COINVENT project adopted this and built systems in mathematics and music.
numbers: Math paper, no empirical data. Notes the COINVENT systems used strict category theory, not the 3/2 version.
limits: Pure theory. Only the introduction and framing were read in detail; proofs not checked.
agent_relevance: Formal view of blending as 'the smallest consistent theory that contains both inputs under a partial mapping'. Gives a precise correctness condition a coded checker could test (mapped axioms still hold in the blend).

source: Ge and Parikh (2021) Visual conceptual blending with large-scale language and vision models, arXiv 2106.14127 - association test
finding: Language models beat a knowledge base at finding a blend partner. Task: predict the property of a simile target from the object, over 66,442 property-object pairs. ConceptNet precision at top 1000 was 5.90; the best language-model row reached 66.38.
numbers: Precision at 10/100/1000 candidates: ConceptNet 1.12 / 2.70 / 5.90; best LM row 2.59 / 24.84 / 66.38; other rows include 0.13 / 7.69 / 37.33 and 1.59 / 15.72 / 53.08. 96.34% of objects found in ConceptNet.
limits: The table's row labels are misaligned in the PDF text, so which model (ELMo, BERT-Base, BERT-Large, GPT) owns which row is uncertain. Test is property prediction from similes, not blend quality. 2021 models.
agent_relevance: LM-first association is far more flexible than a fixed knowledge base for choosing what to blend with. Use it to propose partners; check them with code.

source: Ge and Parikh (2021) human study of image blends from text descriptions
finding: Three image generators were compared on 20 blend descriptions (half from the language-model pipeline, half written by the authors). CLIP-guided BigSleep and DeepDaze beat DF-GAN in pairwise human preference, and BigSleep was preferred over DeepDaze.
numbers: 20 descriptions x 6 questions x 3 model pairs, 9 unique raters per item on Amazon Mechanical Turk. Questions map to the unpacking and integration optimality principles plus interest and aesthetics.
limits: Effect sizes are only shown as a figure (95% bands). Raters judged pictures, not whether the blend solved a task. 2021 models.
agent_relevance: Shows blending can be graded by pairwise preference on the optimality principles; for our agent a cheaper proxy is a code check. Evidence that the output is more useful is absent.

source: Wang, Petridis, Kwon, Ma, Chilton (2023) PopBlends: strategies for conceptual blending with large language models, CHI 2023, arXiv 2111.04920 - Stage 1 accuracy
finding: PopBlends asks GPT-3 for a 'connecting concept' between a pop culture domain and a product. All three prompting strategies (No-GPT, Half-GPT, Full-GPT) gave equally good results; a single try was good about 56% of the time, and the best of five was good about 93% of the time.
numbers: Success per strategy 56.0%, 55.3%, 58.7% (mean 56.7%). At least one good concept among five: 90.0%, 96.6%, 93.3% (93.3% overall). 10 annotators (8 female, mean age 23.7, SD 2.16).
limits: Success judged by 10 student annotators on pop culture and product pairs. GPT-3 (2021 era).
agent_relevance: A generate-5-and-pick-1 design is worthwhile: single try about 57% good, best-of-five about 93%. Code or a separate checker must do the pick.

source: PopBlends (2023) accuracy of GPT-3 entity attributes
finding: GPT-3 invented facts about fictional entities. Attribute accuracy depended on type; catchphrases were often made up.
numbers: Mean rating 2.86 (57% accurate). Adjectives 3.93 (79%), activities 2.89 (58%), catchphrases 1.75 (35%). Inter-rater reliability 0.32 to 0.47 (all 0.41). 10 annotators.
limits: Low rater agreement (IRR 0.41). Fan-wiki ground truth; pop culture domain.
agent_relevance: Direct warning: when the model supplies the facts to blend, about 43% can be wrong. A blend built on invented properties will look fine and fail. Facts must be grounded or checked before projection (G3).

source: PopBlends (2023) Stage 2: scenes related to the connecting concept
finding: Scenes for the connecting concept were generated by GPT-3 (products) or retrieved from fan wikis (pop culture). Product scenes were more often relevant.
numbers: At least one related scene: 98.3% overall. Per scene: product 89.1% (raw 80.0%), pop culture 75.9% (raw 63.4%). Difference 13.2 points.
limits: Two annotators per question. Hallucinated scenes for Star Wars noted in the text.
agent_relevance: Elaboration step (expanding a connection into concrete scenes) works about 8 times in 10 for familiar domains. A coded relevance check is still needed.

source: PopBlends (2023) user study of the full tool vs web search
finding: Within-subjects study: 10 students made six pop culture-product blends, three with PopBlends and three with ordinary search. They produced more than twice as many ideas with PopBlends and reported lower workload.
numbers: Ideas per pair 2.03 (SD 0.84) vs 0.87 (SD 0.56), paired Wilcoxon p < 0.001. NASA-TLX mental demand 2.85 vs 5.80 (W=45, p=0.004), effort W=44, p=0.006, performance 2.10 vs 3.60.
limits: N=10 students, counts of ideas (not rated quality), baseline was web search, not a plain LLM prompt. No test that the blends were better or used.
agent_relevance: Real measured gain for humans from LLM blending support, but the baseline is weak. No comparison with a plain 'think of a blend' prompt, so it does not show the structured pipeline beats one LLM call.

source: Lynn (2026) Conceptual blending in humans and language models, Frontiers in Psychology 17
finding: Conceptual analysis arguing that human blends are goal-driven (goals select which source features project, via affordances) while LLM blends are 'distributionally novel' and steered by proxy-goals from alignment and the prompt. Includes a toy vector-symbolic Python model of goal-conditioned source selection.
numbers: No experiment. Toy example: Osprey tiltrotor (helicopter plus airplane blend for the goal of understanding flight). Claims LLM blends can show interference producing 'generic compromises' when constraints conflict.
limits: Theoretical paper, no measured results, toy model not validated on data. Single author; the LLM claims are argument, not test.
agent_relevance: Practical message for the design: state the goal as a filter on what to project from each input, and keep it explicit in the prompt. Without a goal, blends average out into bland compromises.

source: Sato (2025) The way we prompt: conceptual blending, neural dynamics and prompt-induced transitions in LLMs, arXiv 2505.10948
finding: Maps input space, generic space and blend onto an LLM prompt and output, and defines prompt-induced transitions (tone shifts) and prompt-induced hallucinations (plausible blends of incompatible domains, e.g. periodic table plus tarot). Proposes entropy tracking as a measurement.
numbers: No quantitative results in the text read. Says PIT and PIH can be 'elicited repeatedly' but gives no counts.
limits: Review/position paper; the quantitative claims and cross-model comparison are asserted, not reported. Low evidential weight.
agent_relevance: Useful warning only: blending two distant domains makes a model produce confident, ungrounded text. Treat far-apart blends as high hallucination risk and demand a check.

source: Cho, Zhang, Chen, Inouye (2025) Imagine for me: creative conceptual blending of real images and text via blended attention (IT-Blender), arXiv 2506.24085
finding: An image-generation adapter (built on SD 1.5 and FLUX.1-dev) that blends a real image concept with a text concept. Reports better disentanglement and concept preservation than adapter baselines, and a GPT-4.1 'blending score' with the highest mean and lowest variance.
numbers: SD: 6,000 samples (200 per prompt, 30 prompts) per baseline. FLUX: 4,000 samples (20 prompts) per baseline. GPT-4.1 blending score top mean about 8; low-scoring samples about 1 to 2.
limits: Image domain; scoring by an LLM rubric (self-judging risk). Preprint under review. Not about reasoning.
agent_relevance: Little for a reasoning agent beyond the point that LLM-rubric blend scores are being used as a metric. Under G5 such scores need length and authorship controls.

source: Matsuhira, Kastner, Komamizu, Hirayama, Ide (2024) Investigating conceptual blending of a diffusion model for nonword-to-image generation, ACM MM 2024, arXiv 2411.03595
finding: Stable Diffusion shows blended concepts when two prompts' text embeddings are interpolated. The blend peaks near the midpoint and falls off toward either end.
numbers: At interpolation ratio 0.5: blended-concept depiction (BCD) 0.621 and mixed-concept depiction (MCD) 0.862. Averaged over ratios: BCD 0.389, MCD 0.471. 1,000 concept pairs analysed. Ground-truth embeddings give BCD in up to 60% of images.
limits: Image model; blend detection used an automatic criterion. Not about language reasoning.
agent_relevance: Suggests blends are a matter of weighting, with an optimum near equal weights; a code operator could sweep a weight between a head and a modifier rather than choose one.
